engine_room.deep: An individual component in this group should still have a specific job, source, and evidence. The broad label alone does not explain what any particular mechanism has been shown to do.

entry.label: entry
entry.preview: In the navigation descriptions, an entry is either a starting route or an individual item in a collection.
entry.card: A command described as an entry route helps a reader choose the next relevant action. A glossary or catalog entry instead refers to one stored item with its own identity and detail.
entry.rule: The surrounding noun distinguishes these two common uses.
entry.deep: Plectis tries to make entry routes short enough for first contact while preserving links to the sources needed for the task. An entry should orient the reader before asking them to load deeper context.

epistemic_control_plane.label: epistemic control plane
epistemic_control_plane.preview: The epistemic control plane is a proposed system layer that uses evidence and uncertainty to govern which actions may proceed.
epistemic_control_plane.card: “Epistemic” concerns what is known and how it is justified. The design connects a claim's evidence status to permitted actions, review requirements, and conditions that should stop a change.
epistemic_control_plane.rule: The phrase names a design target associated with the Workingness Instrument; the relevant implementation evidence must be checked separately.
epistemic_control_plane.deep: Its central idea is that changed evidence should change decisions. Recording uncertainty is useful only when the actions that depend on it respond appropriately.

equality.label: equality
equality.preview: An equality states that two expressions represent the same value or mathematical object.
equality.card: For example, 1/2 = 2/4 compares different expressions for the same number. Equality depends on the setting: two functions are equal when they agree as functions, not merely at a few tested inputs.
equality.rule: Distinguish equality from an approximation or a one-way implication.
equality.deep: In Lean, equality is itself a proposition that can require a proof. Two expressions that simplify to the same form may be equal for a more direct reason than expressions requiring a substantial theorem.

equation.label: equation
equation.preview: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal.
equation.card: It can specify a relation, define a quantity, or ask which values make the equality true. For example, x² = 4 has solutions x = 2 and x = −2 over the real numbers.
equation.rule: The permitted domain and assumptions determine what counts as a solution.
equation.deep: Some equations are identities that hold for every allowed value; others hold only for particular values. A displayed equality in a proof may express a justified transformation rather than a problem to solve.

equivalence.label: equivalence
equivalence.preview: Two statements are logically equivalent when each implies the other under the same assumptions.
equivalence.card: To establish P ↔ Q, one proves both P → Q and Q → P. Either statement can then replace the other within that setting, although one may be easier to understand or use.
equivalence.rule: A single implication gives a reduction in one direction, not an equivalence.
equivalence.deep: The papers use equivalences to compare reformulations of open problems. An equivalent reformulation preserves the unresolved question; proving the equivalence alone does not establish either side unconditionally.

erdos.label: Paul Erdős
erdos.preview: Paul Erdős was a mathematician known for work in number theory, combinatorics, probability, and related fields.
erdos.card: He posed and collected many problems, often through extensive collaboration. The site studies selected questions identified by their numbers in the independently maintained Erdős Problems database.
erdos.rule: A database number identifies the question; it does not describe its current solution status.
erdos.deep: Read the linked problem statement and references for the intended formulation. A paper may establish a related theorem, special case, or obstruction while the numbered question remains open.

erdos_problem.label: Erdős problem
erdos_problem.preview: An Erdős problem is a mathematical question associated with Paul Erdős; this site uses the numbering of the Erdős Problems database.
erdos_problem.card: For example, “Erdős #249” identifies a particular database entry rather than the 249th theorem in this repository. The entry supplies the question and references needed to understand its origin and context.
erdos_problem.rule: Compare a paper's exact statement with the original question before interpreting a result as a solution.
erdos_problem.deep: An equivalent reformulation, a finite computation, and an unconditional proof are different forms of progress and should retain their own descriptions.

eulers_theorem_modular.label: Euler's theorem (modular arithmetic)
eulers_theorem_modular.preview: Euler's theorem says that if a is coprime to a positive integer n, then a raised to φ(n) is congruent to 1 modulo n.
eulers_theorem_modular.card: The totient φ(n) counts integers from 1 through n that are coprime to n. For example, φ(10) = 4 and 3⁴ = 81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 10.
eulers_theorem_modular.deep: The exponent φ(n) gives a period but need not be the smallest one. The papers use such exponents to arrange modular repetition while separately proving any claim about the exact multiplicative order.

evaluator.label: evaluator
evaluator.preview: An evaluator is a tool or procedure that assesses something against chosen criteria.
evaluator.card: In Plectis's component model, an evaluator observes inputs and reports its assessment without changing the material being assessed. A separate action is responsible for any repair or update.
evaluator.rule: The criteria determine what its result can establish.
evaluator.deep: For example, an evaluator may detect that a generated page disagrees with source data. Its report identifies the mismatch; it does not by itself decide that the page, source, or generation rule should be changed.

eventual_property.label: eventual property
eventual_property.preview: An eventual property holds at every index after some finite threshold.
eventual_property.card: For a sequence indexed by natural numbers, “eventually P(n)” means that there is an N such that P(n) holds for all n ≥ N. Any failures must occur before that threshold.
eventual_property.rule: This is stronger than holding infinitely often or at arbitrarily large indices.
eventual_property.deep: For example, being positive holds eventually for n − 10, whereas being even never holds eventually for all integers n. The papers use this distinction when comparing recurring obstructions with consequences of rationality.

evidence.label: evidence
evidence.preview: Evidence is information that supports or challenges a particular claim.
evidence.card: It may come from a source, observation, proof, calculation, or recorded test. Plectis links claims to their evidence so readers can examine the basis and decide whether it supports the wording used.
evidence.rule: Evidence should be interpreted within the conditions under which it was obtained.
evidence.deep: A test result, for instance, concerns the version, inputs, and environment tested. A proof has a different scope, determined by its precise statement and assumptions.

evidence_band.label: evidence band
evidence_band.preview: An evidence band labels the kind of support attached to a statement in a mathematical working record.
evidence_band.card: The records use labels such as Lean for formal checking, Cert for a checked certificate, Math for mathematical argument, Cited for a referenced result, and Open for an unresolved obligation.
evidence_band.rule: These labels describe different sources of support, not interchangeable levels of approval.
evidence_band.deep: A separate scope description indicates whether the statement covers listed cases, a bounded range, arbitrarily large parameters, or all allowed parameters. Both the evidence and its reach matter.

exact_rational_arithmetic.label: exact rational arithmetic
exact_rational_arithmetic.preview: Exact rational arithmetic calculates with integer numerators and denominators instead of rounded decimal values.
exact_rational_arithmetic.card: For example, 1/3 + 1/6 is stored and simplified to 1/2 using integer operations. Provided the implementation supports the required integer sizes, these operations introduce no rounding error.
exact_rational_arithmetic.rule: Exact calculation still depends on correct inputs, algorithms, and interpretation.
exact_rational_arithmetic.deep: The papers use it when a tiny difference or precise equality matters. It settles the computed rational expression, while an argument about an infinite limit may also need a proved bound on the omitted terms.

executable_cross_section.label: executable cross-section
executable_cross_section.preview: An executable cross-section is a selected part of a larger system that can be run and inspected on its own.
executable_cross_section.card: Plectis publishes components with the source, inputs, checks, and records needed to examine their behaviour. The selection aims to make a working mechanism available without requiring the entire private environment.
executable_cross_section.rule: Its scope is the included material and the dependencies declared for it.
executable_cross_section.deep: A successful run provides evidence about that public selection. Claims about the larger system need their own support, especially where unpublished components or interactions are involved.

exogenous.label: exogenous
exogenous.preview: Exogenous means originating outside the system or process under discussion.
exogenous.card: An external observation, event, or judgement can be exogenous relative to the process being studied. The classification depends on the chosen boundary: a signal can be external to one component but internal to the organisation containing it.
exogenous.rule: Outside origin does not by itself guarantee accuracy or independence.
exogenous.deep: Plectis uses the term when discussing evidence and criticism that do not arise solely from the workflow producing the work. The source's expertise and dependencies still need assessment.

exogenous_truth.label: exogenous truth
exogenous_truth.preview: “Exogenous truth” is this project's phrase for judgement brought in from outside the process being judged.
exogenous_truth.card: It refers to an independent reader examining the public evidence and forming their own assessment, including disagreement with the project's account. The phrase stresses an external source of criticism or correction.
exogenous_truth.rule: It does not mean that an outsider's judgement is automatically true.
exogenous_truth.deep: The value lies in different evidence, expertise, or assumptions entering the discussion. A claim still needs to be assessed on its merits, whether it comes from inside or outside the project.

exponent.label: exponent
exponent.preview: An exponent specifies a power: in bⁿ, b is the base and n is the exponent.
exponent.card: For a positive integer n, bⁿ means multiplying n copies of b. With nonzero b, b⁰ = 1 and b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ. Fractional and real exponents require further definitions and domain conditions.
exponent.rule: In digit expansions and arithmetic series, check whether the exponent is restricted to integers.
exponent.deep: The expression 2ⁿ − 1 subtracts one after taking the power. It differs from 2ⁿ⁻¹, which lowers the exponent before calculating the power.

exposition.label: exposition
exposition.preview: Mathematical exposition explains a result, its proof, and why the argument works for its intended readers.
exposition.card: Good exposition states the assumptions, introduces notation, identifies the main idea, and distinguishes new work from earlier results. It makes a proof easier to assess and use without weakening its precise claim.
exposition.rule: Clear writing supports verification but cannot replace missing mathematical reasoning.
exposition.deep: The site treats exposition as a separate task from obtaining a checked proof. A formal declaration may be valid while still needing an explanation that lets another mathematician understand or continue the work.

factor.label: factor
factor.preview: A factor is one of the quantities multiplied together to make a product.
factor.card: In 12 = 3·4, both 3 and 4 are factors of 12. For integers, saying that d is a factor of n usually means that d divides n exactly.
factor.rule: Factorisation expresses an object as a product of its factors.
factor.deep: In algebra, factors may be expressions: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1). The setting determines which factors count as irreducible and what uniqueness of factorisation means. Factoring can expose roots or divisibility conditions that are hidden in the expanded expression.

factorial.label: factorial
factorial.preview: The factorial of a nonnegative integer n is the product of the integers from 1 through n, with the value at zero defined as 1.
factorial.card: For example, 4! = 24. Factorials count arrangements of n distinct objects and also provide rapidly growing, highly divisible denominators in number-theory problems.
factorial.rule: The exclamation mark here is mathematical notation, not punctuation indicating emphasis.
factorial.deep: Expressions such as n! − 1 and (n − 1)! have very different values and divisibility properties. The paper's parentheses and order of operations are therefore part of the statement being studied.

factorisation.label: factorisation
factorisation.preview: Factorisation writes a number or algebraic expression as a product of simpler factors.
factorisation.card: For example, 60 = 2²·3·5 is the prime factorisation of 60. Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, apart from the order in which its factors are written.
factorisation.rule: Uniqueness depends on the mathematical setting when the objects are more general than integers.
factorisation.deep: The papers use factorisation to study divisibility, common factors, and the denominators of sums. A convenient factorisation can reveal constraints that are hard to see from a decimal value.

fail_closed.label: fail-closed
fail_closed.preview: Fail-closed means withholding an action when a required condition cannot be established.
fail_closed.card: For example, a publication gate may stop when a required check is missing or its result cannot be read. Plectis uses this behaviour where proceeding without evidence would wrongly treat uncertainty as permission.
fail_closed.rule: The required conditions and the action being withheld must be explicit.
fail_closed.deep: Failing closed can prevent an unsupported action, but it does not prove the underlying artifact is faulty. The next step may be to obtain the missing evidence or repair the check.

failure_class_propagation.label: failure class propagation
failure_class_propagation.preview: Failure-class propagation checks whether a discovered fault also affects other cases for the same reason.
failure_class_propagation.card: Plectis starts with the local failure, identifies its cause, and inspects related surfaces that share the relevant mechanism. Confirmed instances can then be repaired together through the common source or rule.
failure_class_propagation.rule: Similarity alone is not enough to assume that another case has the same fault.
failure_class_propagation.deep: The aim is to fix a recurring cause without expanding the repair to unrelated work. A useful record states which cases were examined and where the explanation stops applying.

failure_modes.label: failure modes
failure_modes.preview: Failure modes are the distinct ways something can fail to meet its intended purpose.
failure_modes.card: A check might accept bad input, reject good input, use stale data, or fail to run. These are different failure modes because their causes, evidence, and repairs can differ.
failure_modes.rule: Name the mechanism of failure, not just the fact that a result is wrong.
failure_modes.deep: Plectis uses negative cases and recorded incidents to make such failures inspectable. Covering known modes improves a check, while new situations may still reveal modes that were not anticipated.

farey_sequence.label: Farey sequence
farey_sequence.preview: The Farey sequence of order N lists all reduced fractions between 0 and 1 whose positive denominators are at most N.
farey_sequence.card: The fractions appear in increasing order, including 0/1 and 1/1. For example, order 3 gives 0/1, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 1/1.
farey_sequence.rule: “Reduced” means that numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than 1.
farey_sequence.deep: The denominator bound makes the sequence finite. Its neighbouring fractions have useful arithmetic relationships, making Farey sequences a way to organise questions about rational approximation and the gaps between fractions.

feedback_loop.label: feedback loop
feedback_loop.preview: A feedback loop occurs when a process's output influences its later behaviour.
feedback_loop.card: Feedback can reinforce a change, counteract it, or create more complicated dynamics. In software, test results can guide revisions; in research, an interpretation can shape which evidence is sought next.
feedback_loop.rule: Feedback is not inherently beneficial or self-confirming; its effect depends on what is measured and how it is used.
feedback_loop.deep: Plectis records evidence and invites external criticism to help distinguish correction from a loop that merely repeats the assumptions of its own earlier outputs.

finite.label: finite
finite.preview: A set is finite if its elements can be counted by a nonnegative integer.
finite.card: In related uses, a finite calculation or sequence has only finitely many steps or terms. The count can be extremely large; finite does not mean practically small or easy to inspect.
finite.rule: Distinguish one large finite case from a statement about every possible size.
finite.deep: The papers may verify many finite instances exactly. Extending that result to all instances requires a general argument, unless a theorem has already reduced the problem to those particular cases.

finite_computation.label: finite computation
finite_computation.preview: A finite computation is a calculation that completes after finitely many steps.
finite_computation.card: It can examine one input or an explicitly bounded collection of cases, producing an exact result or an approximation with stated error. The algorithm and arithmetic determine which kind of result it gives.
finite_computation.rule: The number of cases checked does not by itself extend the result beyond those cases.
finite_computation.deep: A finite computation can support an infinite theorem when combined with a proof of coverage or a suitable error bound. The connection must be stated rather than inferred from the amount of computation.

finite_truncation.label: finite truncation
finite_truncation.preview: A finite truncation keeps a specified finite part of an otherwise longer or infinite object.
finite_truncation.card: For a series, truncating after N terms gives its Nth partial sum and leaves a tail. For a power series, it produces a polynomial retaining a chosen range of powers.
finite_truncation.rule: A finite expression can be calculated exactly while still differing from the full object.
finite_truncation.deep: The papers connect calculations to infinite claims through bounds or identities controlling what was omitted. The truncation point and error estimate determine whether the finite calculation is adequate for the stated conclusion.

fixture.label: fixture
fixture.preview: A test fixture supplies the inputs, state, or environment used for a test.
fixture.card: In Plectis's public examples, fixtures are often small stored datasets or files chosen to exercise particular behaviours. A negative fixture deliberately represents a case the mechanism should reject or report.
fixture.rule: The fixture's role is to make the tested conditions explicit and repeatable.
fixture.deep: Using the same fixture helps comparison, but repeatability also depends on the program and environment. A fixture can test one failure mode well without representing the full range of real-world inputs.

formal.label: formal
formal.preview: Formal means expressed within explicitly specified rules; in mathematics, it usually concerns a precise logical language and inference system.
formal.card: A formal statement identifies its objects and conditions in that language. A formal proof follows the system's rules to derive a conclusion from assumptions.
formal.rule: Precision of form does not ensure that the statement expresses the intended question.
formal.deep: The papers connect formal statements with ordinary mathematical explanations so readers can examine both the validity of the derivation and whether the encoded result matches the claim being made.

formal_mathematics.label: formal mathematics
formal_mathematics.preview: Formal mathematics expresses definitions, statements, and proofs in a language governed by explicit logical rules.
formal_mathematics.card: Proof assistants such as Lean can check the resulting derivations mechanically. Authors may use tactics and automation to construct proofs, while the accepted proof must satisfy the system's checking rules.
formal_mathematics.rule: The exact statement and assumptions determine what has been established.
formal_mathematics.deep: Formal checking reduces dependence on unchecked inference steps. It leaves separate work in choosing the right formulation, explaining the ideas, assessing significance, and ensuring that the formal statement corresponds to the intended mathematics.

formal_proof.label: formal proof
formal_proof.preview: A formal proof is a derivation expressed precisely enough to be checked against a formal system's inference rules.
formal_proof.card: In Lean, a proof establishes a proposition using definitions, earlier results, hypotheses, and any permitted axioms. Automation can construct the proof, but the final object is checked against the claimed type.
formal_proof.rule: A theorem with unresolved hypotheses proves an implication; a theorem using an admission contains an additional proof gap.
formal_proof.deep: The check establishes the encoded statement within its logical setting. Readers still need to compare that statement with the informal result described in the paper.

formal_verification.label: formal verification
formal_verification.preview: Formal verification uses mathematical methods to establish that a system or proof satisfies a precise specification.
formal_verification.card: It can concern software behaviour, hardware, protocols, or mathematical arguments. In the Lean work here, the central check is whether a supplied proof establishes the encoded theorem under its stated assumptions.
formal_verification.rule: The specification and trusted checking machinery are part of the guarantee.
formal_verification.deep: A formally verified result may still address the wrong specification or an incomplete model of the intended problem. Explaining and reviewing that correspondence remains necessary alongside the mechanical check.

formalisation.label: formalisation
formalisation.preview: Formalisation translates mathematical definitions, statements, and arguments into a precise formal language.
formalisation.card: The work includes choosing representations, making implicit assumptions explicit, and filling in steps required by the proof assistant. The resulting objects can then be checked by the formal system.
formalisation.rule: A faithful formalisation must preserve the meaning and scope of the original mathematics.
formalisation.deep: Sometimes the process exposes a missing hypothesis or an ambiguous argument. It can also prove useful supporting results, which should be distinguished from the main theorem when describing what the project contributes.

fraction.label: fraction
fraction.preview: A fraction writes a quotient as a/b; for a rational number, a and b are integers and b is nonzero.
fraction.card: The numerator a is divided by the denominator b. Different fractions can represent the same number: 2/4 and 1/2 are equal because the common factor 2 can be cancelled.
fraction.rule: “In lowest terms” means that numerator and denominator are coprime.
fraction.deep: An expression written as a quotient is not necessarily a rational number if its numerator or denominator is non-integer. For example, √2/1 is still irrational.

freshness.label: freshness
freshness.preview: Freshness describes whether stored information still reflects the source or state it is meant to represent.
freshness.card: A generated page, cached result, or copied file may have been accurate when created and become outdated after its source changes. Plectis uses source versions and refresh rules to assess that relationship.
freshness.rule: A recent timestamp alone does not show that the right source was read.
freshness.deep: A useful freshness record identifies the source, the version examined, and the condition that requires another check. Different kinds of information can have very different refresh needs.

front_end.label: frontend
front_end.preview: A front end is the part of a software system through which a user interacts with it.
front_end.card: It may present screens, controls, and views over data supplied by a back end. In the site's “Why” walkthrough, the term refers to the larger system's operator interface shown in the videos.
front_end.rule: That demonstrated interface has a different scope from the public website you are reading.
front_end.deep: Both can present views of related source objects. Their appearance alone does not establish which actions or private data are available through each interface.

frontier.label: frontier
frontier.preview: Here, the mathematical frontier is the stated boundary between established results and unresolved questions for a problem.
frontier.card: A useful account identifies the strongest relevant results, the assumptions still needed, and the approaches that have been ruled out. It helps another researcher choose a next question without reconstructing all earlier work.
frontier.rule: A convenient intermediate target is not automatically equivalent to the original problem.
frontier.deep: Moving the frontier requires a meaningful mathematical change, such as removing a hypothesis or proving a new obstruction. More declarations or a new presentation alone do not show that change.

function.label: function
function.preview: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain.
function.card: It comes with a domain of allowed inputs and a codomain in which outputs lie. For example, f(n) = n² defines a function from the integers to the integers.
function.rule: Different inputs may have the same output; one input cannot have two outputs under the same function.
function.deep: In the papers, domain restrictions are part of the definition. A formula involving division, logarithms, or roots may define different functions depending on which inputs are permitted.

gate.label: gate
gate.preview: A gate is a checkpoint that permits an action only when specified conditions are satisfied.
gate.card: Plectis uses gates before changes or publication that require evidence, such as a successful check or a matching source version. The gate records which requirement determined its decision.
gate.rule: A gate's pass means that its particular conditions were met.
gate.deep: It cannot establish requirements that it never examines. A blocked gate can indicate missing evidence, a failing check, or an unavailable dependency, and those cases may require different next steps.

generalise_up_propagate.label: generalise-up-propagate
generalise_up_propagate.preview: Generalise-up-propagate means turning a supported local lesson into guidance that future relevant work will actually encounter.
generalise_up_propagate.card: Plectis first identifies what the case teaches and how broadly the lesson applies. It then places the refinement in an existing rule, skill, standard, or other source used by the affected workflow.
generalise_up_propagate.rule: A single example should not become a universal rule without an argument for that scope.
generalise_up_propagate.deep: The change should preserve the source case and its limits. Updating the shared owner can prevent repeated mistakes more effectively than adding another isolated note.

geometric_majorant.label: geometric majorant
geometric_majorant.preview: A geometric majorant bounds terms or their magnitudes by a geometric sequence with a fixed ratio.
geometric_majorant.card: If |a_N₊ₖ| ≤ Crᵏ for k ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ r < 1, the entire tail's absolute sum is at most C/(1 − r). This turns infinitely many bounds into a usable finite estimate.
geometric_majorant.rule: The same ratio and initial bound must work throughout the claimed tail.
geometric_majorant.deep: Rapidly growing factorial denominators can supply such comparisons. The starting index matters because a ratio bound may fail for early terms even when it holds for all later ones.

geometric_series.label: geometric series
geometric_series.preview: A geometric series adds terms formed by repeatedly multiplying an initial value by a fixed number.
geometric_series.card: Its terms are a, ar, ar², and so on, where a is the initial value and r is the common multiplier. When |r| < 1, the infinite sum is a/(1−r); for example, 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 2.
geometric_series.rule: For a nonzero initial value, the infinite sum converges exactly when |r| < 1. With initial value zero, every term and the sum are zero.
geometric_series.deep: Geometric series and their differentiated forms give explicit bounds for analytic tails and their first and second derivatives in the lemniscate paper.

git.label: Git
git.preview: Git is a version-control system that records snapshots of files and the history connecting them.
git.card: A commit identifies a stored snapshot, its parent history, and a message. Branches name lines of development, and differences between commits show how tracked content changed.
git.rule: Uncommitted edits are part of a working copy, not yet part of a recorded commit.
git.deep: The repositories use Git revisions to identify the source behind a paper, check, or generated page. Sharing a revision lets another person obtain the same tracked content rather than an unspecified current copy.

github.label: GitHub
github.preview: GitHub is a service for hosting Git repositories and tools for collaboration around them.
github.card: It provides interfaces for browsing files and history, discussing issues, reviewing changes, and publishing releases. GitHub Pages can serve static websites from a repository's published content.
github.rule: Git is the version-control system; GitHub is one service that hosts repositories using it.
github.deep: The links on this site lead to public source and related artifacts. A hosted file's presence establishes availability, while its correctness and evidence status must be assessed from the work itself.

govern.label: govern
govern.preview: To govern a process is to define how its decisions are made, authorised, and checked.
govern.card: In Plectis, this includes assigning source authority, setting rules for changes, and specifying evidence required before an action proceeds. The relevant rule should be discoverable where the action is performed.
govern.rule: A written rule and an enforced rule are different states of implementation.
govern.deep: To assess a governed process, inspect both its stated contract and the mechanism applying it. Recorded decisions can then show whether the rule had the intended effect in a particular case.

greatest_common_divisor.label: greatest common divisor
greatest_common_divisor.preview: For integers not all zero, the greatest common divisor is the largest positive integer dividing every one of them.
greatest_common_divisor.card: The common positive divisors of 12 and 18 are 1,2,3,6, so gcd(12,18)=6. Two integers are coprime exactly when their gcd is 1.
greatest_common_divisor.rule: Signs do not affect the nonnegative gcd. By convention gcd(0,0) = 0, and gcd(a,0) = |a|; these cases require care when describing the gcd as a largest positive divisor.
greatest_common_divisor.deep: The factorial paper uses gcds to measure cancellation, reduce denominators, and control how prime factors overlap across many terms.

grounding.label: grounding
grounding.preview: Grounding connects a statement or decision to the information that gives it meaning and support.
grounding.card: For a factual claim, that may be a source or observation. For a system term, it may be the code and records defining its local use. Plectis expects important explanations to retain those connections.
grounding.rule: The source must be relevant to the actual claim, not merely related to its subject.
grounding.deep: A source link improves inspectability but does not settle interpretation by itself. The reader still needs to check that the source supports the wording and scope.

guinea_pig.label: guinea pig
guinea_pig.preview: “Guinea pig” is an informal term for a person or case on which an experimental method is tried.
guinea_pig.card: The phrase draws attention to who bears the uncertainty, inconvenience, or consequences of the trial. In descriptions of this project, it concerns the experience of trying an unfinished workflow or method.
guinea_pig.rule: An experimental use should be understood through its actual conditions and limits.
guinea_pig.deep: The metaphor does not establish that a method works or that its effects generalise. A trial can reveal useful failures while leaving wider effectiveness and suitability unresolved.

harness.label: harness
harness.preview: A test harness is the code and setup that runs a test and captures its result.
harness.card: It supplies inputs, prepares the environment, invokes the thing being tested, and records or compares outputs. Plectis uses harnesses to make a component's advertised check executable.
harness.rule: The harness is separate from both the component and the claim being tested.
harness.deep: Its own behaviour matters: a harness that runs the wrong command or ignores a failure can produce a misleading pass. Negative cases help check that relevant failures are actually detected.

hologram.label: hologram
hologram.preview: In Plectis, “hologram” means a structured, compressed view that preserves routes into the material it summarises.
hologram.card: Public JSON packets carry selected content, identities, and relationships so an assistant or reader can examine the collection without reconstructing the website page by page. Internal navigation uses the same idea at different levels of detail.
hologram.rule: The term is a project metaphor, not a claim about optical holography.
hologram.deep: The packet's declared coverage determines what it contains. Source links and preserved relationships make deeper inspection possible even when the packet deliberately omits large bodies of detail.

html.label: HTML
html.preview: HTML is the markup language used to describe the structure and meaning of web-page content.
html.card: Elements identify headings, paragraphs, links, lists, forms, and other parts that browsers and assistive technology can interpret. CSS controls presentation, while JavaScript can add behaviour.
html.rule: HTML structure affects how a page works as well as how it looks.
html.deep: The site's glossary references are links to definitions, enhanced with interactive previews. Keeping meaningful links in the page lets readers still reach an entry when the preview script is unavailable.

hypothesis.label: hypothesis
hypothesis.preview: A mathematical hypothesis is an assumption under which a statement is being considered or proved.
hypothesis.card: For example, “if n is prime and greater than 2, then n is odd” assumes both primality and the size condition. The conclusion is asserted for cases satisfying those assumptions.
hypothesis.rule: A hypothesis in a theorem need not be an unproved conjecture; it may simply define the cases covered.
hypothesis.deep: In conditional research results, a particular hypothesis may remain unresolved. The proof then establishes what follows from it, rather than establishing that it holds.

ide.label: IDE
ide.preview: An IDE, or integrated development environment, is an application combining tools for working on software.
ide.card: It commonly provides a code editor, project navigation, diagnostics, and ways to build or run programs. Support for a proof language can also show goals, errors, and declaration information while a proof is developed.
ide.rule: An IDE is useful for local work but is not required to read the website.
ide.deep: The repositories' command-line checks describe the reproducible operations. An editor interface can invoke or help inspect those operations without replacing their recorded inputs and results.

implication.label: implication
implication.preview: An implication says that if one statement holds, another follows.
implication.card: The notation P → Q means “if P, then Q”. P is a sufficient condition for Q, and Q is a necessary condition for P. This alone does not say that Q implies P.
implication.rule: Proving the implication does not establish P itself.
implication.deep: The papers use implications to connect hypotheses and target results. To claim an equivalent reformulation, the reverse implication must also be proved under compatible assumptions.

inequality.label: inequality
inequality.preview: An inequality compares quantities using an order relation such as <, ≤, >, or ≥.
inequality.card: The symbol ≤ means “less than or equal to”, so x ≤ M allows x to equal M. The strict inequality x < M excludes equality.
inequality.rule: The difference between strict and non-strict bounds can determine whether an endpoint is included.
inequality.deep: Inequalities in the papers often control an error or bound a sum. Each manipulation must respect sign conditions: multiplying both sides by a negative number reverses the order.

infinite.label: infinite
infinite.preview: An infinite set has more elements than any finite set; no finite count exhausts it.
infinite.card: Infinite sequences and series specify a term for every index in an unending index set. Statements about them are expressed through definitions, quantifiers, and limits rather than by carrying out infinitely many steps.
infinite.rule: “Infinitely many” is weaker than “all” and can also be weaker than “all sufficiently large”.
infinite.deep: For example, there are infinitely many even integers, but arbitrarily large odd integers remain. This distinction matters when interpreting the scope of a theorem.

inspection.label: inspection
inspection.preview: Inspection means examining the actual material closely enough to assess a specific question about it.
inspection.card: Here that can involve reading a theorem statement, tracing its proof dependencies, examining a test, or comparing a result record with the command that produced it. The relevant depth depends on the question.
inspection.rule: Reading a summary is useful orientation but may leave the decisive detail unexamined.
inspection.deep: Plectis provides source and evidence routes to make that deeper reading possible. Inspection can reveal uncertainty as well as confirm a claim; it need not end in approval.

integer.label: integer
integer.preview: An integer is one of the numbers …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … .
integer.card: Integers have no fractional part. They include positive and negative whole numbers and zero, and are usually denoted collectively by ℤ.
integer.rule: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication preserve integers; division need not do so.
integer.deep: Number-theory statements often restrict integers further, for example to positive or nonnegative values. Those restrictions matter for divisibility, factorials, and sequence indices, so they are part of the mathematical claim rather than optional wording.

integral_curve.label: integral curve
integral_curve.preview: An integral curve of a vector field is a parametrised curve whose velocity agrees with that field at every point.
integral_curve.card: It solves x′(t) = V(x(t)). For the constant field V = 1 on the real line, the curves are x(t) = t + c, with the starting value determined by c.
integral_curve.rule: Existence and uniqueness require conditions on the field, such as local Lipschitz continuity for a standard uniqueness theorem.
integral_curve.deep: In the Newton-flow papers, the field is regular away from zeros of p′. A trajectory approaching an excluded point needs separate analysis before further continuation can be asserted.

intelligent.label: intelligent
intelligent.preview: Intelligent ordinarily describes an ability to learn, reason, understand, or adapt to a task.
intelligent.card: The word covers several capacities rather than one universally agreed measure. Performance can vary with the problem, available context, tools, and time.
intelligent.rule: Plectis's Type A and Type B labels describe access and authority, not intelligence.
intelligent.deep: An actor may reason well while lacking access to the evidence needed for a particular claim. Conversely, permission to run commands gives an opportunity to gather evidence without guaranteeing good judgement about the results.

invariant.label: invariant
invariant.preview: An invariant is a quantity or property preserved by specified transformations or steps of a process.
invariant.card: For example, repeatedly adding 2 preserves an integer's parity. The unchanged property can connect distant stages without examining every intermediate operation separately.
invariant.rule: An invariant is preserved exactly in the stated sense; a quantity merely increasing or decreasing is instead monotone.
invariant.deep: The papers use preserved arithmetic relationships to constrain possible trajectories of a recurrence. Which transformation is allowed matters: a property invariant under one update need not survive a different operation or change of coordinates.

irrational.label: irrational
irrational.preview: A real number is irrational if it cannot equal a/b for any integers a and nonzero b.
irrational.card: For example, √2 is irrational. In any fixed integer base greater than one, an irrational number's digit expansion never becomes permanently periodic.
irrational.rule: An infinite expansion alone does not imply irrationality: 1/3 has an infinite repeating decimal expansion.
irrational.deep: An irrationality proof must rule out every possible rational representation. Computing many digits or checking many candidate denominators can provide evidence, but it does not on its own exclude all fractions.

irrationality_criterion.label: irrationality criterion
irrationality_criterion.preview: An irrationality criterion is a proved condition that can be used to establish that a number is irrational.
irrationality_criterion.card: It may require a pattern of rational approximations, denominators, or scaled tails that a rational number cannot have. The criterion gives a route to irrationality when its requirements are verified.
irrationality_criterion.rule: Some criteria are sufficient conditions; stronger characterisations give both necessary and sufficient conditions.
irrationality_criterion.deep: The papers state these logical roles separately. Proving a criterion is useful, but applying it to an open problem still requires establishing the condition for the particular number under study.

kernel.label: kernel
kernel.preview: A kernel is a system's central core; this site uses the word for both Lean's proof checker and Plectis's command router.
kernel.card: The Lean kernel checks proof objects against the formal language's rules. Plectis's `kernel.py` instead answers questions about the repository and directs agents towards relevant files, records, and actions.
kernel.rule: The surrounding discussion of proofs or navigation identifies which meaning applies.
kernel.deep: The two programs have different responsibilities and guarantees. A route returned by Plectis's kernel is navigation information, while acceptance by the Lean kernel concerns the validity of a specific encoded proof.

laboratory.label: laboratory
laboratory.preview: In Plectis, a laboratory is a controlled setting for trying a proposed mechanism before relying on it in live work.
laboratory.card: It runs candidate checks, rules, or workflows against selected fixtures and records what happens. The small, explicit setting makes it easier to investigate failures and compare proposed changes.
laboratory.rule: Laboratory evidence covers the experiment that was actually run.
laboratory.deep: A successful trial can justify further testing or a proposed integration. It does not automatically change a governing rule or establish that the mechanism will behave the same way on every live input.

lambert_series.label: Lambert series
lambert_series.preview: A Lambert series has the form ∑ aₙxⁿ/(1 − xⁿ), usually summed over positive integers n where it converges.
lambert_series.card: At x = 1/b, its terms become aₙ/(bⁿ − 1). Expanding the denominators as geometric series connects the coefficients to sums over divisors, under conditions that justify rearranging the terms.
lambert_series.rule: A power series ∑ aₙxⁿ is a different expression and is not automatically a Lambert series.
lambert_series.deep: That distinction matters here: the totient power series and the sums with denominators bⁿ − 1 are related number-theory objects, but their definitions and convergence arguments must be read separately.

latex.label: LaTeX
latex.preview: LaTeX is a system for writing structured documents that a typesetting engine turns into formatted output, usually a PDF.
latex.card: Authors write text together with commands for sections, equations, references, and layout. This is widely used for mathematical papers because complex notation and cross-references can be maintained in source form.
latex.rule: The source file and rendered document serve different purposes and should correspond to the same version.
latex.deep: The site publishes readable paper views alongside source material where available. A successful typesetting run checks document construction, not the correctness of the mathematics.

lattice.label: lattice
lattice.preview: In Plectis, the lattice is the network of relationships between rules, skills, concepts, code, and evidence.
lattice.card: Its connections state how items relate: a standard may govern a skill, a component may implement a mechanism, and a record may support a claim. This lets a reader follow meaning across different kinds of artifact.
lattice.rule: This project usage does not assert the axioms of a mathematical lattice.
lattice.deep: In order theory, a lattice instead requires a greatest lower bound and least upper bound for every pair. The local term is a name for the system's relationship graph.

lattice_transposition.label: lattice transposition
lattice_transposition.preview: Lattice transposition moves a reusable lesson into the kind of system record that can apply it to future work.
lattice_transposition.card: A local failure may reveal a missing instruction, validation rule, or concept. Plectis retains the original case and places the general refinement in the narrowest existing skill, standard, or other owner that can carry it.
lattice_transposition.rule: The lesson's scope must survive the move.
lattice_transposition.deep: For example, a faulty glossary preview may justify changing the shared glossary rule. It does not automatically justify changing how every kind of document is written.

launch_scope_decision.label: launch-scope decision
launch_scope_decision.preview: A launch-scope decision determines what is ready and authorised to be published or made available.
launch_scope_decision.card: It considers the intended audience, included material, evidence, and unresolved limitations. In Plectis, component checks provide information for this decision but do not independently grant publication authority.
launch_scope_decision.rule: A passing technical check answers its own conditions, not every question about release readiness.
launch_scope_decision.deep: The person responsible for the release must make the decision within the authorised scope. A published selection should then match the material and evidence on which that decision was based.

lay_person.label: lay person
lay_person.preview: A lay person is someone who is not a specialist in the subject being discussed.
lay_person.card: The term concerns subject knowledge, not intelligence or general ability. A mathematician can be a lay reader of software architecture, just as an experienced programmer can be new to number theory.
lay_person.rule: The glossary aims to explain unfamiliar terms without requiring specialist training.
lay_person.deep: Readers can still contribute useful questions, corrections, or work with tools. Specialist judgement may be needed for particular claims, and the project should make that need clear rather than assume a reader's background.

lean.label: Lean
lean.preview: Lean is a programming language and proof assistant used to state mathematics and check formal proofs.
lean.card: Authors supply definitions, theorem statements, and proofs, often with tactics that help construct the proof object. Lean then checks that the object establishes the encoded proposition under its assumptions.
lean.rule: Successful checking applies to that precise formal statement.
lean.deep: Admissions, added axioms, or an incorrectly translated problem can limit what acceptance establishes. The papers therefore need readable statements and evidence of the relevant checks alongside the Lean source.

lean_kernel.label: Lean kernel
lean_kernel.preview: The Lean kernel is the core that checks whether a formal proof object has the type claimed for it.
lean_kernel.card: Proof-writing tools and tactics help construct objects that the kernel checks according to Lean's logical rules. This separates proof search from the final checking operation.
lean_kernel.rule: Acceptance depends on the encoded statement, definitions, and axioms used by the proof.
lean_kernel.deep: The kernel does not judge whether that statement captures an informal conjecture or whether a result is significant. Those questions require mathematical interpretation and review of the correspondence with the paper.

lean_standard_axioms.label: Lean's standard axioms
lean_standard_axioms.preview: Lean's usual mathematical foundations include propositional extensionality, quotient soundness, and classical choice.
lean_standard_axioms.card: Their names are `propext`, `Quot.sound`, and `Classical.choice`. They support standard mathematical reasoning in Lean and Mathlib. An axiom audit identifies which assumptions a particular declaration depends on.
lean_standard_axioms.rule: “No added axioms” here means no assumptions beyond the allowed mathematical foundations, not that the proof uses no axioms at all.
lean_standard_axioms.deep: Lean also exposes mechanisms such as `sorryAx` for unfinished proofs. These must be distinguished from the permitted foundations when checking whether a result has proof gaps.

least_common_multiple.label: least common multiple
least_common_multiple.preview: For positive integers, the least common multiple is the smallest positive integer divisible by all of them.
least_common_multiple.card: For example, the least common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12. In prime factorisation, it keeps the highest exponent of each prime appearing in the inputs.
least_common_multiple.rule: Positivity matters because zero is also a common multiple but is not the intended minimum here.
least_common_multiple.deep: Least common multiples combine periodic conditions: an event repeating every 4 steps and one repeating every 6 steps align every 12 steps. Definitions involving zero or empty collections need their stated conventions.

lebesgue_measure.label: Lebesgue measure
lebesgue_measure.preview: Lebesgue measure generalises length on the real line, area in the plane, and volume in higher dimensions.
lebesgue_measure.card: For an interval it gives the usual length, but it also applies to many fragmented or irregular sets. A set can contain infinitely many points and still have measure zero.
lebesgue_measure.rule: Claims using Lebesgue measure apply to measurable sets in the stated space.
lebesgue_measure.deep: The papers use it to distinguish the size of a set from its number of points or its topological shape. Positive measure, containing an interval, and being infinite are different properties.

lemma.label: lemma
lemma.preview: A lemma is a proved statement introduced mainly to support another argument.
lemma.card: It has the same need for a valid proof as a theorem. The label describes its role in the exposition, not a lower standard of correctness or a guarantee that it is easy.
lemma.rule: Read its hypotheses before applying it to a later step.
lemma.deep: A lemma may isolate the main difficulty, provide a reusable technical fact, or organise a long proof. Counting lemmas therefore gives little information by itself about the number of distinct mathematical ideas.

lemniscate.label: lemniscate
lemniscate.preview: A polynomial lemniscate is a set defined by the size of a complex polynomial, commonly the curve |p(z)| = c.
lemniscate.card: The term is also used, with qualification, for a sublevel region such as |p(z)| < c or |p(z)| ≤ c. These regions can have several components surrounding the polynomial's roots.
lemniscate.rule: Check whether the paper means the level curve, the open region, or the filled closed region.
lemniscate.deep: In the Erdős #1041 material, paths inside the open unit region |p(z)| < 1 are central. Being on its boundary is different from being inside it.

level_set.label: level set
level_set.preview: A level set consists of all points where a function has one specified value.
level_set.card: For a real-valued function g, the level set at c is {x : g(x) = c}. In the plane, g(x,y) = x² + y² has a unit circle as its level set at 1.
level_set.rule: A level set need not be a smooth curve; critical points can produce singularities or changes of shape.
level_set.deep: Polynomial lemniscates use g(z) = |p(z)|. Their level curves are different from the regions defined by |p(z)| < c or |p(z)| ≤ c.

limit.label: limit
limit.preview: “Limit” can mean a restriction or, in mathematics, the value approached by a sequence or function.
limit.card: On the system pages, a scope limit states how far a claim or action reaches. A service limit instead restricts use of a resource. Mathematical limits describe behaviour as an input approaches a point or infinity.
limit.rule: The surrounding phrase determines which meaning applies.
limit.deep: For a mathematical example, 1/n tends to the limit zero as n increases, although every term is positive. The separate mathematical-limit entry explains that precise sense in more detail.

lineage.label: lineage
lineage.preview: Lineage records where an item came from and which transformations led to its present form.
lineage.card: For a generated page, it may identify source records, the builder, and the relevant versions. For a claim, it may connect an interpretation to earlier results or observations.
lineage.rule: Origin and correctness are separate questions: a traceable item can still contain an error.
lineage.deep: Plectis uses lineage to make copies and summaries inspectable. When a source changes, those connections help identify which derived artifacts may need to be rebuilt or reconsidered.

living_system_posture.label: living system posture
living_system_posture.preview: Living system posture means treating claims about a changing system as statements about an identifiable state or version.
living_system_posture.card: A report can remain a valid record of an earlier run after the implementation has changed. Plectis distinguishes that historical record from evidence about the system as it exists now.
living_system_posture.rule: The relevant source and refresh rule determine whether an old observation still applies.
living_system_posture.deep: This does not make every mathematical theorem time-dependent. It concerns facts such as which proof version was checked, which files were published, or which behaviour a particular run demonstrated.

locus.label: locus
locus.preview: A locus is a place where something occurs or is defined; in mathematics, it can mean all points satisfying a condition.
locus.card: In the system documentation, a code locus identifies the file or function implementing a behaviour. In geometry, the locus of points at distance one from the origin is the unit circle.
locus.rule: The subject determines whether the word means a source location or a mathematical set.
locus.deep: Both uses help make a description precise: they replace an unspecified “somewhere” with a location or condition that can be examined directly.

logarithm.label: logarithm
logarithm.preview: For a positive base b other than 1, the real logarithm log_b(x) is the exponent y satisfying bʸ = x, for x > 0.
logarithm.card: For example, log₂(8)=3 because 2³=8. In advanced mathematics, log without a base usually means the natural logarithm with base e.
logarithm.rule: For positive inputs, logarithms turn products into sums and real powers into multipliers: log(xy) = log x + log y and log(xᵃ) = a log x. Complex logarithms require separate branch choices.
logarithm.deep: The papers take logarithms of products and least common multiples to compare multiplicative growth efficiently using additive estimates and asymptotic scales.

machine_checked.label: machine-checked
machine_checked.preview: Machine-checked means software has verified a stated property of the supplied material.
machine_checked.card: The strength of that verification depends on the checker. A Lean kernel check concerns a formal proof; a schema check concerns a file's structure; a test run concerns behaviour on particular inputs.
machine_checked.rule: Always identify what was checked and by which method.
machine_checked.deep: The phrase alone does not mean that every surrounding claim is true. The encoded statement, assumptions, source version, and connection to the informal explanation determine how far a mathematical checking result reaches.

manifest.label: manifest
manifest.preview: A manifest is a structured inventory of the files or objects included in a build, package, or release.
manifest.card: It may record paths, versions, content digests, sizes, and relationships. Plectis uses such inventories to describe what a published collection contains and to support consistency checks.
manifest.rule: The manifest's listed content should agree with the actual files.
manifest.deep: A manifest helps detect missing, unexpected, or changed artifacts. It does not itself establish the correctness of their contents, and its own source and generation process need to remain identifiable.

map.label: map
map.preview: A map presents a collection and the relationships that help someone navigate it.
map.card: Plectis's software maps are generated views of stored objects, such as components and their dependencies. The view lets a reader choose a part before opening its detailed sources.
map.rule: In a mathematical passage, “map” commonly means a function instead.
map.deep: For a generated system map, completeness depends on what the underlying analysis captures. Links to source and a refresh record help readers understand both the represented relationships and the limits of the view.

mathematical_continuity.label: mathematical continuity
mathematical_continuity.preview: A function is continuous when sufficiently close inputs always produce sufficiently close outputs.
mathematical_continuity.card: For a function between metric spaces, continuity at x means that every output tolerance ε > 0 has an input tolerance δ > 0: whenever y is less than δ from x, f(y) is less than ε from f(x). For real or complex functions, these distances are written |y−x| and |f(y)−f(x)|.
mathematical_continuity.rule: Continuity allows bending and changing speed but forbids jumps. A continuous path is a continuous function from an interval into the space being studied.
mathematical_continuity.deep: The lemniscate problem requires a path whose every point stays inside {|f|<1}; continuity makes it one unbroken connection between the selected roots.

mathematical_induction.label: mathematical induction
mathematical_induction.preview: Mathematical induction proves a claim for every natural-number index by establishing a starting case and a valid step to the next case.
mathematical_induction.card: The step assumes the claim for an arbitrary index n and proves it for n + 1. Together with the base case, that gives the claim throughout the stated range.
mathematical_induction.rule: The starting index and induction hypothesis must match the statement being proved.
mathematical_induction.deep: Strong induction allows the step to use all earlier cases. The papers use these methods to establish recurrence formulas, divisibility propagation, and finite identities later used in arguments about limits.

mathematical_limit.label: mathematical limit
mathematical_limit.preview: A mathematical limit describes the value a sequence or function approaches as its index or input approaches a specified point or infinity.
mathematical_limit.card: For a real sequence with limit L, every positive tolerance around L eventually contains all later terms. The terms need not ever equal L; 1/n tends to zero while staying positive.
mathematical_limit.rule: The limit and the value at a particular input are different concepts.
mathematical_limit.deep: For functions, the relevant domain and direction of approach matter. An argument about an infinite sum uses the limit of its finite partial sums.

mathematical_priority.label: mathematical priority
mathematical_priority.preview: Mathematical priority concerns who first established or discovered a result, as supported by the scholarly record.
mathematical_priority.card: It can involve dated manuscripts, publications, communications, and careful comparison of what each source actually proved. Closely related results may have different hypotheses, conclusions, or forms of contribution.
mathematical_priority.rule: The project's own contribution records cannot settle an unresolved priority question by declaration.
mathematical_priority.deep: When this site says it asks for no priority on someone else's solution, it means using the project as a starting point does not give the project authorship of that person's result.

mathematician.label: mathematician
mathematician.preview: A mathematician studies mathematical structures and questions through definitions, reasoning, and proof.
mathematician.card: The term covers many specialisms and forms of work, including research, teaching, exposition, and applications. Expertise relevant to one paper may differ from the expertise needed for another.
mathematician.rule: The site invites mathematical judgement about correctness, context, significance, and useful next questions.
mathematician.deep: A contribution may clarify a proof, identify prior work, refute a proposed step, or find a new result. Its value depends on the work itself rather than on agreement with the project's current direction.

mathematics.label: mathematics
mathematics.preview: Mathematics studies patterns, quantities, structures, and relationships through precise definitions and logical reasoning.
mathematics.card: Its results are established by proof, while examples, computation, and conjectures help discover what might be true. The mathematical pages here focus on selected problems associated with Erdős and related formal work in Lean.
mathematics.rule: That collection is one research programme within a much wider subject.
mathematics.deep: The site distinguishes proved results, finite calculations, conditional arguments, and open questions so readers can understand what each artifact contributes without treating every mathematical-looking output as a theorem.

mathlib.label: Mathlib
mathlib.preview: Mathlib is the community-maintained library of mathematical definitions, theorems, and tools for Lean.
mathlib.card: It supplies reusable material across many fields, along with notation and tactics that help authors build further proofs. A local project can import the relevant modules instead of developing all foundations itself.
mathlib.rule: The Mathlib version is part of a formal project's reproducible environment.
mathlib.deep: Using a theorem from the library requires matching its assumptions and types. New declarations built on Mathlib should distinguish the project's contribution from results already supplied by the library.

mechanism.label: mechanism
mechanism.preview: A mechanism explains how an outcome is produced through particular inputs, steps, and interactions.
mechanism.card: In Plectis, a useful mechanism description names what enters, what happens, what comes out, and which conditions constrain the process. This connects a conceptual explanation to implementation and evidence.
mechanism.rule: A label for a capability is not yet an account of how it works.
mechanism.deep: For example, “detects drift” becomes inspectable when the description identifies the two sources compared, the comparison rule, and the record produced when they disagree.

mechanism_contract.label: mechanism contract
mechanism_contract.preview: A mechanism contract states what a component is expected to do and how that expectation can be checked.
mechanism_contract.card: It identifies the component's purpose, inputs or conditions, outputs, evidence, and scope limits. Plectis uses this information on component cards so readers can inspect different mechanisms with a consistent set of questions.
mechanism_contract.rule: The contract states the expectation; source and execution evidence show whether it is met.
mechanism_contract.deep: If the implementation or supported use changes, the contract needs to be reviewed with it. A broader description should not inherit evidence collected for an earlier, narrower behaviour.

mersenne_number.label: Mersenne number
mersenne_number.preview: A Mersenne number has the form 2ⁿ − 1 for a positive integer n.
mersenne_number.card: The sequence begins 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. Some are prime, but many are composite; “Mersenne prime” is the more specific term for a prime of this form.
mersenne_number.rule: In base two, 2ⁿ − 1 is written as n consecutive ones.
mersenne_number.deep: The Erdős #257 material studies reciprocal sums involving these denominators. Expressions bⁿ − 1 use a similar construction at another base, but the unqualified name Mersenne conventionally refers to base two.

metabolism.label: metabolism
metabolism.preview: “Metabolism” is Plectis's name for the recurring work that keeps stored knowledge and generated views in step with their sources.
metabolism.card: The process identifies changes, queues bounded work, refreshes affected artifacts, and records the checks. It covers upkeep such as rebuilding an index or incorporating a supported lesson into an existing rule.
metabolism.rule: The biological word is a metaphor for maintenance and renewal in the software.
metabolism.deep: The process should have explicit owners and stopping conditions. A refresh that runs successfully still needs to preserve source meaning and satisfy the checks governing its output.

metadata_only.label: metadata-only
metadata_only.preview: Metadata-only means a record contains information about material or a run without including the underlying bodies themselves.
metadata_only.card: It may list counts, identifiers, classifications, digests, and outcomes while omitting the source text or inputs. This can make a record smaller or limit what it discloses.
metadata_only.rule: The omitted content may still be necessary to independently inspect or repeat the work.
metadata_only.deep: A digest can identify a file but cannot reconstruct it. A metadata-only result therefore needs an appropriate source route if readers are expected to examine the evidence behind its verdict.

microcosm.label: Microcosm
microcosm.preview: Microcosm is an earlier public name for Plectis that remains in some technical paths and compatibility identifiers.
microcosm.card: Existing package names, schemas, files, and links may retain the old spelling to preserve compatibility and traceability. Current reader-facing descriptions use Plectis for the project.
microcosm.rule: The presence of the old name does not by itself identify a separate project or release.
microcosm.deep: An ordinary phrase such as “a microcosm of a larger system” has a different meaning: a small representative example. The glossary keeps that everyday sense separate from this historical project identifier.

mining.label: mining
mining.preview: Here, “mining” means sustained searching through candidate arguments and experiments for useful mathematical results or failures.
mining.card: A person or agent follows a research direction, tries approaches, checks candidates, and preserves useful outcomes. The term describes repeated exploration rather than a single answer to a prompt.
mining.rule: The amount of computation does not determine the value of what is found.
mining.deep: Results still need verification, explanation, and attribution. A failed approach can be useful when it records a precise obstruction, while many unchecked drafts may add little to the understanding of a problem.

model.label: model
model.preview: A model is a representation used to describe, predict, or reason about something.
model.card: Here the word often refers to an AI model used by an agent. In mathematics, a model may instead be a structure satisfying a theory's axioms; in software, a data model specifies how information is organised.
model.rule: The surrounding qualifier identifies the intended meaning.
model.deep: An AI model is only one part of an agent's working setup. Tools, instructions, available evidence, and permissions also affect what the agent can do and what its answers can establish.

module.label: module
module.preview: A module is a unit of code or written material organised around a subject or responsibility.
module.card: A code module groups related definitions and exposes interfaces to other code. A Plectis paper module explains a subsystem and links its concepts, implementation, and evidence.
module.rule: The module's dependencies determine what else is needed to understand or use it.
module.deep: The same word also has a separate algebraic meaning, generalising a vector space from a field to a ring. That mathematical use must be read from its own definitions and context.

modulus.label: modulus
modulus.preview: In modular arithmetic, the modulus is the positive integer that determines which remainders are distinguished.
modulus.card: Modulo 5, integers fall into five classes represented by 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Changing the modulus changes these classes and the divisibility information they retain.
modulus.rule: In a complex-number passage, “modulus” instead means magnitude: |z| is the distance of z from zero.
modulus.deep: Both meanings occur in these papers. A phrase such as “critical-value modulus” refers to a complex magnitude, while “modulo m” refers to arithmetic with integer remainders.

monic.label: monic
monic.preview: A polynomial is monic if its leading coefficient is 1.
monic.card: The leading coefficient multiplies its highest-degree nonzero term. For example, z³ + 2z − 7 is monic, while 3z³ + 2z − 7 is not.
monic.rule: This normalisation concerns the polynomial's scale, not the positions of its roots alone.
monic.deep: In lemniscate questions, multiplying a polynomial by a constant changes sets defined by |p(z)| < 1 or |p(z)| = 1. A monic hypothesis therefore matters to geometric statements about those sets.

morse_saddle.label: Morse saddle
morse_saddle.preview: A Morse saddle is a critical point of a smooth real-valued function whose second-order form is nondegenerate and has both positive and negative directions.
morse_saddle.card: In two dimensions, the local behaviour resembles x² − y² after a suitable change of coordinates: the value rises in some directions and falls in others. Nondegeneracy rules out flat second-order directions.
morse_saddle.rule: At a planar saddle, the level set through the point has four local half-branches.
morse_saddle.deep: The lemniscate arguments use this local geometry. It must be distinguished from the behaviour of a singular flow or a degenerate critical point, where additional analysis is required.

multiple.label: multiple
multiple.preview: In arithmetic, a multiple of an integer d is a number d·k for some integer k.
multiple.card: For example, 12 is a multiple of 3 because 12 = 3·4. A common multiple of several positive integers is divisible by every one of them.
multiple.rule: The adjective “multiple” also means “more than one” in ordinary prose.
multiple.deep: In phrases such as “multiple root”, it has a more specific algebraic role: a root occurs with multiplicity greater than one. The surrounding noun therefore matters when reading this word in a paper.

multiple_root.label: multiple root
multiple_root.preview: A multiple root of a nonzero polynomial is a root appearing with multiplicity at least two.
multiple_root.card: For example, z² − 2z + 1 = (z − 1)² has 1 as a double root. In general, multiplicity k means (z − a)ᵏ divides the polynomial but the next power does not.
multiple_root.rule: Over the real or complex numbers, every multiple root is also a root of the derivative.
multiple_root.deep: This changes local geometry and root counting. A polynomial's degree counts roots over the complex numbers with multiplicity, while the number of distinct root locations can be smaller.

multiplicative_order.label: multiplicative order
multiplicative_order.preview: For b coprime to a positive modulus Q, the multiplicative order is the least positive k for which bᵏ ≡ 1 modulo Q.
multiplicative_order.card: It measures the repetition period of powers of b in modular arithmetic. For example, the order of 2 modulo 7 is 3, since 2³ leaves remainder 1 and no smaller positive exponent does.
multiplicative_order.rule: Finding an exponent with remainder 1 gives a period, which need not be the least one.
multiplicative_order.deep: Exact order requires a minimality argument. The papers use this distinction when connecting denominator arithmetic with periodic digit patterns and finite certificates.

named_basis.label: named basis
named_basis.preview: A named basis identifies the exact inputs, assumptions, or sources on which a claim rests.
named_basis.card: Plectis uses the phrase to make a result reproducible and inspectable: the supporting material should be specified precisely enough for another checker or reader to examine it.
named_basis.rule: This is a statement of support, distinct from a vector-space basis in linear algebra.
named_basis.deep: A path without a version may not identify the bytes used in an earlier run. Source revisions, content digests, and explicit hypotheses help preserve the intended basis as files and explanations change.

natural_number.label: natural number
natural_number.preview: A natural number is a counting number; in Lean, the natural numbers include zero: 0, 1, 2, 3, … .
natural_number.card: Mathematical authors differ on whether their notation ℕ starts at zero or one. Lean's type `Nat` starts at zero, and positivity must be stated separately when needed.
natural_number.rule: Check the convention in a paper rather than inferring it from the phrase alone.
natural_number.deep: This matters for factorials, denominators, and sequence indices. A theorem valid for positive n may need a separate hypothesis or a separate zero case when encoded over `Nat`.

navigation.label: navigation
navigation.preview: Navigation is the process of finding and moving between relevant parts of a body of information.
navigation.card: Plectis provides collections, summaries, search, links, and command routes to help a reader reach the source needed for a task. Different levels of detail let the reader narrow the question before opening large files.
navigation.rule: Navigation should preserve the identity and meaning of the selected object across views.
navigation.deep: A good route reduces unnecessary reading while keeping evidence accessible. It cannot replace the underlying material when the task requires checking a claim or changing an implementation.

necessary_and_sufficient.label: necessary and sufficient
necessary_and_sufficient.preview: A condition is necessary and sufficient for a statement when each implies the other.
necessary_and_sufficient.card: Necessary means the statement cannot hold without the condition. Sufficient means the condition guarantees the statement. Together they give an equivalence, often written “if and only if” or ↔.
necessary_and_sufficient.rule: A condition can have one of these roles without having the other.
necessary_and_sufficient.deep: For example, divisibility by 4 is sufficient for an integer to be even but is not necessary: 6 is even. Distinguishing the directions prevents a stronger research target from being mistaken for the original problem.

negative_case.label: negative case
negative_case.preview: A negative case is a test input designed to exercise a failure or refusal that the system should detect.
negative_case.card: It accompanies valid inputs so a checker cannot appear successful simply by accepting everything. Plectis may plant a forged result, missing action, or invalid condition and verify that the appropriate finding is produced.
negative_case.rule: The expected response must be stated for the particular case.
negative_case.deep: Rejecting one planted error supports that detection path. It does not establish that every possible error will be detected, and valid inputs are also needed to check for inappropriate refusals.

neighbourhood.label: neighbourhood
neighbourhood.preview: A set containing an open set around a specified point or subset.
neighbourhood.card: For a point x in the plane, any set containing a small open disc centred at x is a neighbourhood of x. Its size may depend on x.
neighbourhood.rule: Authors sometimes say neighbourhood for the open disc itself and sometimes for any set containing one; the common content is local room around the target.
neighbourhood.deep: The paper needs neighbourhoods where analytic expansions converge and saddle geometry has a controlled local form before connecting it to global paths.

newton_flow.label: Newton flow
newton_flow.preview: For a complex polynomial p, the Newton flow studied here follows the differential equation z′ = −p(z)/p′(z) where p′(z) ≠ 0.
newton_flow.card: It is a continuous analogue of Newton's root-finding iteration. Along a regular trajectory, the chain rule gives d(p(z(t)))/dt = −p(z(t)), so the polynomial value decays exponentially.
newton_flow.rule: The displayed vector field is undefined at critical points where p′ vanishes.
newton_flow.deep: This limitation matters in the lemniscate arguments: local trajectories and their behaviour near critical points require separate justification. The decay identity applies only along intervals where the trajectory is defined and p′ does not vanish.
